title: How Bats Find Their Way
text: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly, and most of them come out at night. There are more than a thousand kinds of bat, from tiny bats no bigger than a bumblebee to giant fruit bats with wings over a metre wide. In the dark, it is almost impossible to see, so most bats that hunt insects use a clever trick to find their way. This trick is called echolocation.

As a bat flies, it makes high-pitched squeaks that are too high for people to hear. The sounds travel through the air until they hit something, such as a tree, a wall or an insect. Then the sound bounces back to the bat as an echo.

The bat’s large ears catch the echo. Its brain works out how long the sound took to return. A short delay means the object is close, while a longer delay means it is further away. The pattern of the echo also tells the bat what shape the object is and whether it is moving.

Using echolocation, some bats can find a tiny moth in complete darkness. As the bat gets closer to its prey, it makes its squeaks faster and faster, like a drummer speeding up. This gives the bat a more and more exact picture of where the moth is. Some moths have learned to fight back. They can hear the bat’s squeaks and dive towards the ground to escape.

Some bats spend the whole day hanging upside down in caves, then leave together in huge groups at sunset. With thousands of bats squeaking at once, you might think they would get confused, but each bat seems able to pick out its own echoes from all the noise.

Echolocation also stops bats from crashing into things. They can even dodge a thin wire! Without this skill, a bat flying through a dark forest would keep hitting the trees. Scientists believe that echolocation helps bats to survive, because it allows them to hunt when there are fewer predators around and less competition for food.

People have copied the bat’s trick. Ships use a machine called sonar to send out sounds and listen for the echoes. By timing the echoes, sailors can find out how deep the sea is and whether there are rocks ahead. Dolphins also use echolocation, sending clicks through the water to find fish. It seems that nature invented the idea long before we did.

title: The Pea That Did Not Matter
text: Queen Marguerite of Thornbury had one strict rule for choosing a bride for her son, Prince Callum: the girl must be a true princess. “A true princess has such delicate skin,” the Queen liked to declare, “that she can feel a single pea beneath twenty mattresses.” Nobody had ever dared to argue with her, although several courtiers had privately wondered whether it was true.

One drizzly evening, a young woman knocked at the castle door, her boots caked in mud and her cloak soaked through. “My name is Nell,” she said. “My cart has lost a wheel on the road, so please may I shelter in your barn tonight?” The Queen looked her up and down before whispering to the maid, “She insists that she is not a princess, but that is exactly what a clever princess would say.”

Dot, the maid, was instructed to place a pea at the very bottom of a tall tower bed and to pile twenty soft mattresses on top of it. Dot did as she was told, more or less. Then Nell climbed the ladder, yawned, and was fast asleep before the candle had stopped smoking.

At breakfast, the Queen leaned forward eagerly. “Tell me, my dear, did you feel anything strange in the night?” Nell stretched contentedly. “I slept like a log,” she replied. “I have slept in haystacks, on ferry decks and once in a wheelbarrow, so that was the softest bed I have ever known.” The Queen was so dismayed that she dropped her spoon into her porridge.

Prince Callum, who had been listening from the doorway, burst out laughing. “Mother, Nell has travelled all the way from the coast,” he said. “She mends carts and sells honey in every village along the road, so of course she was tired!” Nell held out a small jar. “This is to say thank you for the bed.” Then, very quietly, Dot cleared her throat. “Your Majesty, I must confess something. I took the pea out, because the poor girl looked so weary that it did not seem fair.”

For a long moment, nobody spoke. Then the Queen tasted a spoonful of honey and, to everyone’s astonishment, she smiled. “It is very good honey,” she admitted. “Perhaps I have been asking the wrong question, because a pea cannot tell me whether someone is kind.” That afternoon, the Prince and Nell mended the broken cart wheel together, while the pea was planted in the castle garden, where by summer it had grown into a tall, leafy plant covered in sweet green pods.

title: Our Neighbours in Space
text: The Solar System is made up of the Sun and everything that travels around it. The Sun is a star, a giant ball of hot, glowing gas, and its pull is so strong that it holds eight planets in orbit around it. An orbit is the curved path that one object follows as it travels around another. The Sun’s light is so far away that it takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.

The four planets closest to the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. They are made mostly of rock, and they are small compared with the planets further away. Mercury is the closest to the Sun and the fastest mover, completing one orbit in just 88 days. Venus, however, is the hottest planet. Its thick clouds trap heat like a blanket, so its surface is hotter than an oven. Mars is known as the red planet because its soil contains rusty iron.

Beyond Mars lie the giants. Jupiter is the biggest planet of all, and more than a thousand Earths could fit inside it. It is made mostly of gas, so there is no solid ground to stand on. Saturn is famous for its rings, which are made of ice and rock. The pieces range from tiny specks to large chunks. Saturn is also very light for its size. Scientists say that it would float in water, if anyone could find a bath big enough!

Uranus and Neptune are the two planets furthest from the Sun. They are freezing cold places that are very hard to spot from Earth, and they look blue because of a gas called methane in the air around them. Because they are so far out, they take a very long time to travel around the Sun. One year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years.

How do we know so much about worlds we cannot visit? Scientists send spacecraft called probes. Probes have flown past every planet in the Solar System, taking photographs and measuring what they find. A probe called Voyager 2 was launched in 1977, and it is still the only one to have visited Uranus and Neptune. Its journey shows that, even in space, there is always something new to discover.

title: The Rules of the Den
text: By Saturday morning, the den beneath Yusuf’s apple tree was finally finished. It had taken three weekends, two balls of string and a great deal of arguing, but the walls of old pallets stood firm, and a blue tarpaulin stretched across the top like a roof. Yusuf’s best friends, Poppy and Tomasz, stepped back to admire it.

“Right,” said Poppy, producing a crumpled sheet of paper from her pocket. “Every proper den needs rules. Rule one: members only. Rule two: nobody enters without the password. Rule three: no little brothers or sisters.” She glanced pointedly towards the house, where Yusuf’s sister Zara was watching through the kitchen window.

Yusuf felt his face grow warm. “Zara is only six,” he muttered. “She has been helping me carry things all month.” “That is exactly the problem,” said Poppy. “She will touch everything and tell the whole street our password.” Tomasz shuffled his feet and studied the grass, clearly wishing that he were somewhere else.

“It is my garden,” said Yusuf. “It was my idea,” said Poppy. For several minutes neither of them would give way, and the silence between them grew as heavy as the clouds gathering above the apple tree.

The first drops of rain settled the argument, though not in the way anyone expected. Within seconds the wind had whipped the tarpaulin free at one corner, and it flapped wildly, threatening to tear the whole roof away. The three friends grabbed at it, but the rope kept slipping through their cold, wet fingers.

Then Zara appeared, wearing her wellingtons and a raincoat two sizes too big. Without a word, she scrambled underneath, took the rope from Yusuf and looped it round a pallet in a neat, tight knot. “Our Beavers leader showed me,” she said. “It is called a clove hitch, and it never comes undone.” She tied the other three corners in exactly the same way, and the tarpaulin stopped flapping.

Crouched inside the dry, dim den, listening to the rain drumming on the roof, Poppy glanced at her crumpled list. Slowly, she took a pencil, crossed out the third rule and scribbled something new underneath. “Rule three,” she read aloud, a little sheepishly. “Anyone who can tie a proper knot is welcome.” Zara beamed so widely that Yusuf could not help grinning too.

title: A River’s Journey
text: Every river begins as a small trickle of water. This starting place is called the source, and it is often high in hills or mountains. Some rivers begin instead at a lake or a boggy patch of ground. Here, rain that has soaked into the ground bubbles out as a spring and begins to run downhill. Rivers always flow downhill because gravity pulls water towards the lowest ground.

Near the source, the river is narrow, shallow and fast, because the slope is steep. Even a small stream can be surprisingly powerful when it is moving quickly. The rushing water carries stones and pebbles that scrape at the river bed and banks. Over thousands of years, this wears away the rock and carves a V-shaped valley. Waterfalls can form where the river tumbles over a hard ledge of rock.

As the river travels on, smaller streams called tributaries join it, so it grows wider and deeper. The land becomes flatter, and the river slows down and begins to bend. On the outside of each bend, the water flows faster and wears away the bank. On the inside, the water flows more slowly, so it drops mud and sand. Over time, the bends grow into large loops called meanders.

Near the end of its journey, the river is wide and slow, and it flows so gently that it hardly seems to move at all. It carries fine mud called silt. After heavy rain, a river may burst its banks and spread across the flat land on either side, which is known as the floodplain. When the water drains away, it leaves a layer of silt behind. Silt is full of goodness that plants need, so floodplains often have some of the richest soil for growing crops.

Finally, the river reaches its mouth, where it flows into a sea or a lake. The water does not stay there for ever. The Sun’s heat turns water from the surface into an invisible gas called water vapour. This is called evaporation. High in the sky, the vapour cools and forms clouds. When the clouds become heavy, the water falls as rain, and it soaks into the hills once more. The journey then begins again. This never-ending journey is called the water cycle.

title: Mum’s Saturday Secret
text: For three weeks, Mum had been disappearing every Saturday morning. She always said the same thing, “Just popping out,” and she always came back at lunchtime with sawdust in her hair. My twin sister, Aaliyah, and I had a theory. “Mum has a secret,” Aaliyah whispered, “and it is a woodwork one.”

Aaliyah kept a list of clues in her notebook. Clue one was the sawdust. Clue two was a paintbrush we found hidden behind the sofa. Clue three was Dad, who whistled cheerfully whenever we asked a question, and who always seemed to be standing in front of the loft ladder. “Nothing to see here!” he would say. It was the worst pretending I had ever seen.

On the Saturday before our birthday, Grandma arrived early with a bag of sandwiches. “I am taking you both to the park for the morning,” she announced. “Not a word to your mother.” We fed the ducks and ate all the sandwiches, but Aaliyah kept glancing at her watch. “They are up to something,” she muttered.

When we got home at one o’clock, Mum and Dad tied scarves over our eyes and led us up the stairs. I could hear the ladder creak. “Ready?” asked Mum. Then the scarves fell away, and my heart was racing.

I did not recognise the loft. The dusty boxes had gone. In their place stood tall bookshelves painted sunshine yellow, a heap of squashy cushions, and a round window that let in a beam of light. The whole room glowed like the inside of a lantern. Above the door, a hand-painted sign read, “Aaliyah and Daniel’s Library.”

“I built the shelves at Uncle Rob’s workshop,” said Mum, brushing her hair. “That is where the sawdust came from. I wanted you to have somewhere quiet to escape to when the world feels too loud.” I could not say a single word. Aaliyah found a brand-new book with both our names inside the cover, and she hugged it to her chest.

“Someone has to test the beanbags,” said Dad, and he flopped down first. We spent the whole afternoon reading. Before bed, Aaliyah opened her notebook and, under her list of clues, wrote two words in capital letters: “MYSTERY SOLVED.”

title: The Final Leg
text: The stadium was much bigger than Kai had imagined. Rows of empty seats curved around the running track, and the loudspeaker crackled as an announcer read out the names of schools from all over the district. Kai gripped the cold metal baton until his knuckles turned pale. He was the last runner in the Year 6 relay, and he could not stop thinking about last Tuesday, when he had fumbled the baton in practice and it had clattered across the tarmac.

“Breathe,” said Mr Bell, the coach, crouching beside him. “Your job is simple. Take the baton, run as fast as you can, and trust your legs.” Kai nodded, though his stomach felt like a washing machine. Behind him, Grace, Omar and Priya were shaking out their arms and jogging on the spot. Grace would run first because she had the quickest start. Omar and Priya would follow, and Kai would take the final stretch.

The whistle blew, and Grace shot away like a released spring. By the time she reached Omar, Elm Park were lying second. Omar ran steadily, but on the third leg a tall boy from Hillcrest swept past him, and the gap began to widen. Priya dug in her heels and pushed with every ounce of strength she had. When she arrived at the changeover, Elm Park were in third place, only a few metres behind the leaders.

“Go, Kai!” Priya gasped. He was already moving, one arm stretched out behind him, his eyes fixed on the track ahead. For a heartbeat he felt nothing. Then the baton slapped perfectly into his palm. The roar of the crowd seemed to fade away, and everything he had feared vanished, replaced by the steady thump of his trainers on the track.

On the final bend, Kai overtook the runner in front. Now only one boy stood between him and the finish line, and the boy was tiring. Ten metres. Five metres. Kai lunged for the tape at the same moment as the leader, but the leader crossed first, by no more than a whisker.

Kai bent over with his hands on his knees, gasping for breath. Then Grace crashed into him with a hug, and Omar and Priya piled in behind. “Second!” Grace shouted. “In the whole district!” Mr Bell hurried over, beaming. “Every changeover was perfect,” he said. “That is the hardest part of a relay, and you nailed it.” Kai looked down at the silver medal hanging around his neck. He realised that, for the whole of the last leg, he had not once thought about dropping the baton.

title: The Human Heart
text: The human heart is a muscle about the size of your clenched fist, and it never takes a rest. It beats without you ever having to think about it. It sits in the middle of the chest, slightly to the left, and is protected by the ribs. Its job is to pump blood around the body. Blood carries oxygen, a gas from the air we breathe, and goodness from our food to every part of us. Without a constant supply, the body’s cells could not work.

Inside, the heart has four hollow spaces called chambers. The two upper chambers are known as atria, and the two lower chambers are known as ventricles. Blood first flows into the atria. Next, the ventricles squeeze hard to push it out. As they squeeze, small flaps called valves shut, so that the blood cannot slip backwards. Then the ventricles relax, and the whole cycle starts again. The valves work like tiny doors that open one way only. The “lub-dub” sound that a doctor hears through a stethoscope is the sound of the valves closing.

Blood travels through tubes called blood vessels. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins carry it back. The finest tubes are the capillaries, which are thinner than a hair, and they reach every corner of the body. A single drop of blood can travel all the way around the body in about a minute.

When an adult is resting, the heart beats roughly 70 times a minute. That adds up to more than 100,000 beats every day. Children’s hearts are smaller and usually beat a little faster. During exercise, the muscles need extra oxygen, so the heart speeds up to deliver it. You can feel each beat as a pulse in your wrist or neck. If you count the beats for one minute, you have measured your heart rate. Your heart rate also rises when you feel excited or nervous, which is why your heart may thump before a race.

Like any muscle, the heart grows stronger with exercise. A stronger heart can pump more blood with each beat, so it does not need to beat as often when the body is resting. This is why athletes often have slower resting heart rates than other people. Eating a balanced diet and sleeping well also help to keep the heart healthy. Doctors also recommend that children get plenty of active play every day.

title: A Day at a Victorian School
text: In the 1880s, a law made school compulsory for children aged between five and ten. Before then, many children had worked in fields or factories instead. Families often paid a few pennies each week for a child’s lessons, and this continued until 1891. A day at a typical village school began early and followed strict routines.

Children arrived by half past eight. Many had walked several miles, and boys and girls often entered by separate doors. When the bell rang, everyone lined up in silence. The teacher inspected each child for clean hands and tidy clothes before allowing them inside.

The classroom was crowded. A single teacher might teach fifty children of different ages, with the help of older pupils called monitors. Children sat in rows on hard wooden benches, facing the front. Younger pupils wrote with chalk on small slates, which could be wiped clean and used again because paper was expensive. Older pupils practised writing with a dip pen and a pot of ink, and blots were common.

The morning was for “the three Rs”: reading, writing and arithmetic. Pupils chanted their spelling and their times tables aloud until they knew them by heart. Learning by repeating was thought to be the best way of remembering. Anyone who chattered or daydreamed might be made to stand at the front of the room while the class carried on.

At midday, the children ate a simple lunch brought from home, usually bread and cheese, often sitting on the ground in the yard. They played outside, skipping with ropes, spinning wooden tops or rolling hoops along the ground. There were no toys with batteries or screens, so children made up their own games.

After lunch, the girls often practised needlework, sewing samplers with tiny, neat stitches, while the boys might do drill or drawing. On some afternoons, the school held a lesson called object lessons, where the teacher showed a real item, such as a piece of coal or a seashell, and asked questions about it.

By four o’clock, the children lined up once more to say a prayer and to recite a poem before going home. Many hurried off to help with jobs such as feeding animals or fetching water. It was a long day, but for many children, it was the first time that they had ever been taught to read.

title: The Harbour Before Sunrise
text: The harbour is still asleep when I arrive, wrapped in a blanket of cool, grey half-light. Nothing moves except the water, which slaps softly against the stone wall and slides away again, over and over, like someone breathing in their sleep. The air tastes of salt and rope and cold metal, and my breath hangs in front of me in small white clouds.

Along the quay, the boats bob at their moorings in tidy rows. There are rowing dinghies painted in faded reds and blues, a squat little ferry with a striped funnel, and a tall sailing boat whose mast rocks slowly from side to side, ticking against its ropes like a clock. Each boat has a name lettered on its stern in curling gold paint: Wren, Sea Biscuit, Marigold. I wonder who chose them, and whether they still remember why.

Then the sky begins to change. First, a thin line of pale pink creeps along the horizon, as if someone were drawing it with a fine pencil. Slowly the line widens and deepens, spilling orange across the clouds and washing the whole bay in a glow the colour of apricots. The windows of the tall, narrow houses on the hill catch the light one by one, and they flash as though they were waking up and winking at the sea.

Now the harbour begins to stir. A gull lands on a bollard and lets out a harsh, scornful cry, and within seconds the air is full of white wings and squabbling. Somewhere behind me a door bangs, and the smell of warm bread drifts down from the bakery at the end of the lane. A man in a yellow jacket strolls along the quay, jangling a bunch of keys. He unlocks the hatch of the ferry, and the engine coughs, splutters and then settles into a low, comfortable purr.

By the time the sun finally lifts clear of the water, everything has changed. The grey has melted away, and the harbour blazes with colour: the red of the dinghies, the gold of the lettering, the deep green of the weed on the steps. Even the puddles on the cobbles are shining. I sit on the edge of the wall with my feet dangling and my hands wrapped round a warm bread roll, and I decide that this is the best hour of the whole day.

title: Why Every School Needs a Garden
text: Imagine a school where the playground has a corner full of beans, sunflowers and buzzing insects, and where pupils sometimes learn with soil on their hands. This is not a dream. Many schools already have gardens, and there are strong reasons why every school should do the same.

Firstly, a garden is a living classroom. Children can see for themselves how a seed becomes a plant, and how bees carry pollen from flower to flower. Lessons in science, maths and writing become far more memorable when they are linked to something real. Measuring the height of a sunflower or weighing a harvest of potatoes is much more exciting than working from a book.

Secondly, gardens can help pupils to eat more healthily. Studies suggest that children are more willing to try vegetables they have grown themselves. A pupil who might refuse a carrot at lunch may happily crunch one that they have pulled out of the ground and washed in the school sink.

Thirdly, gardening is good for our wellbeing. Digging, watering and weeding are calm activities that give children a break from screens and noise. Being outdoors in the fresh air can help pupils to feel more relaxed, and many find it easier to concentrate afterwards. A garden also teaches patience, since plants cannot be hurried.

Finally, gardens help nature and bring people together. Flowers and shrubs provide food for bees, butterflies and birds, and a small pond can become a home for frogs. Working together to look after a plot teaches teamwork, because every job, from planting to picking, needs someone to do it.

Some people argue that school gardens cost too much money and take up valuable lesson time. However, a garden does not need to be expensive. Seeds are cheap, and tools can be donated by families or local shops. Nor does it need to be big: a few raised beds or even some containers on a windowsill are enough to begin. As for lesson time, gardening is not an extra. It can be part of the lessons children are already having.

In conclusion, a school garden helps children to learn, to eat well, to feel calm and to care for the world around them. With so many benefits and so few drawbacks, it is hard to see why any school would say no. Every school should plant a garden and watch it grow.

title: The Night the Tent Came Down
text: Zainab had packed the rucksack herself, and she was rather proud of it. It held torches, spare socks, a bag of marshmallows and, tucked into a side pocket, a small repair kit that Grandad had pressed into her hand before they left. “You never know,” he had said. Zainab had rolled her eyes, but she had packed it anyway.

By late afternoon, Dad and her younger brother Idris had put up the tent in a sheltered corner of the campsite, right beside a chattering stream. They cooked sausages on the stove, toasted the marshmallows until they were black and gooey, and watched the sun slip behind the hills. When it grew dark, the three of them wriggled into their sleeping bags and lay listening to the water. “This,” murmured Dad, “is the life.”

Zainab woke suddenly in the middle of the night. The tent walls were flapping like enormous wings, and the wind was howling around the campsite. Then came a sharp crack, and one side of the tent folded slowly inwards, draping cold, damp fabric over her face. “Dad!” squealed Idris. “Everyone stay calm,” said Dad, fumbling for the torch. “A pole has snapped, that is all.”

There was no question of mending it in the dark. Dad bundled the children into their sleeping bags, carried them across the field one at a time, and settled them on the back seat of the car, where the wind could not reach them. Rain began to patter on the roof. Idris fell asleep almost at once, but Zainab lay awake, thinking about the tent and about the little kit in her rucksack.

By morning the wind had died, and the sky had turned a clean, rinsed blue. The tent lay crumpled on the grass like a giant, deflated balloon, with the broken pole poking out at a sorry angle. Dad scratched his head. “We may have to go home,” he said. “I cannot see how to fix that.”

“Wait,” said Zainab. She fetched the repair kit and unrolled it on the grass. Inside lay a short metal sleeve, exactly the right width, and a roll of strong tape. She slid the sleeve over the crack, as Grandad had once shown her, and wound the tape tightly round it until the pole stood straight again. Dad stared. Then, very slowly, he began to laugh.

By breakfast time the tent was standing once more, a little crooked but perfectly sound. Zainab sat in the sunshine with a bowl of steaming porridge, and Idris held out a marshmallow on a stick. “Next time,” said Dad, “you are in charge of the packing.” “Next time,” grinned Zainab, “I am also in charge of the tent.”

title: The Canoe on Crane Lake
text: Ravi and his cousin Elsie had waited the whole year for the canoe trip. Their uncle Tomas, who managed the outdoor centre on Crane Lake, had promised that this summer they could paddle out to Heron Island by themselves. “Hug the shore until you reach the reeds,” he said, handing them each an orange life jacket, “and after that it is a straight line across. You will be there in twenty minutes.” Then he pressed a small compass into Elsie’s palm. “Just in case,” he added, with a wink.

The lake lay flat and silver in the early light, and the canoe glided over it almost without a sound. Ravi sat at the front and Elsie at the back, and their paddles dipped in perfect time while a pale mist hung low over the water. Heron Island was a dark smudge on the horizon, and it seemed to grow larger with every stroke.

Halfway across, however, the mist thickened until it rolled over the surface in heavy white folds, swallowing the shore behind them and then the island ahead. Ravi turned his head this way and that, but there was nothing to see except grey. “Which way now?” he asked. Elsie stopped paddling. “I thought you were watching the island,” she said. “I was,” Ravi replied, “right up until it vanished.”

Then Elsie remembered the compass in her pocket. “Uncle Tomas said the island lies north-east of the jetty,” she said slowly. “If we follow the needle, we ought to reach it.” She balanced the compass on her knee and waited while the needle trembled and finally settled. Ravi noticed that her hands were not quite steady, although her voice sounded perfectly calm. “Steer us that way,” she said, “and I will tell you whenever we begin to drift.”

It was slow, careful work. Ravi counted his strokes aloud in a voice that was a little thinner than usual, and after every fifty strokes Elsie checked the needle. Somewhere in the whiteness a heron called, and both cousins jumped so violently that the canoe wobbled. The minutes stretched out, and Ravi began to wonder whether they had chosen the wrong direction after all.

Just as his arms began to ache, a row of dark pine trees loomed out of the mist, and the front of the canoe scraped onto a beach of small grey pebbles. Ravi let out an enormous breath, and Elsie began to laugh, softly at first and then so helplessly that the canoe rocked beneath them. Far behind them, a horn sounded across the water. Uncle Tomas had seen the mist rolling in from the jetty, and he was already on his way to find them.
“Next time,” said Ravi, wiping his forehead, “I will watch the compass as well as the island.” Elsie shook her head, smiling. “Next time,” she said, “we both will.”

title: The Mill at the Bottom of the Sea
text: Long ago, in a cold northern land of steep fjords and dark pine forests, there lived a fisherman named Anders, who was so poor that in some winters his family had nothing to eat but turnips and a little stale bread. One morning, while he was mending his nets on the shore, a stranger with a long grey beard stopped beside him and studied him thoughtfully. “You look like a man who shares whatever he has,” said the stranger. “I have a gift for you.”

From beneath his cloak he drew a small stone mill, no bigger than a loaf of bread, and placed it in the fisherman’s hands. “Turn the handle and speak your wish,” he explained. “The mill will keep grinding for as long as you please, but when you have enough, you must say, ‘Stop, mill, stop,’ and it will rest.” Before Anders could thank him, the stranger had vanished, leaving only a line of footprints in the sand.

Anders tried the mill at once. “Grind me a loaf of bread,” he whispered, and as he turned the handle, out tumbled a warm, golden loaf. Within days his table was piled high with cheese, apples and herrings. Yet Anders never kept the bounty to himself; each week he shared it generously with his neighbours, and the village had never been so cheerful.

News of the mill spread across the fjords and eventually reached the ears of a ship’s captain named Borg, a shrewd man who was also extremely greedy. He longed to possess the mill, and on a moonless night he crept into Anders’s cottage and carried it away to his ship. As soon as they were safely out at sea, he turned to his crew with a satisfied grin. “Now we shall never go hungry,” he declared. “What shall we ask for? Salt! We can sell it for a fortune.”

“Grind me salt,” he ordered, turning the handle. White crystals began to pour out, and the crew cheered. But Borg had never troubled to ask how the mill was stopped, and now he could not recall a single word of what he had overheard. The salt gushed faster and faster, rising around the sailors’ boots and then up to their knees. “Stop!” shouted Borg. “Halt! Enough!” But the mill paid no attention.

The ship sank lower and lower beneath its glittering burden. Just in time, Borg and his crew scrambled into a small rowing boat and paddled away, coughing and blinking. Behind them the great ship slid beneath the waves, and the little mill went down with it, still grinding.
Some people say that the mill lies on the sea floor to this very day. It has never found the words to make it stop, and so it goes on making salt, which is why, they say, the sea tastes salty.

title: Dumplings for the New Year
text: Every year, on the last evening before the New Year, the whole of Mei-Ling’s family squeezed into her grandmother’s tiny flat to make dumplings together. Aunts, uncles and cousins arrived clutching mixing bowls and rolling pins, and Po Po, Mei-Ling’s grandmother, presided over the kitchen like a general commanding an army. This year, for the first time, Mei-Ling was considered old enough to help.

“Watch my hands,” said Po Po, laying a circle of dough on Mei-Ling’s palm. She dropped a spoonful of pork and chives into the centre, folded the dough over, and pinched the edge into a row of neat little pleats, as swiftly as a bird tucks in its wing. “Now you try.”

Mei-Ling’s first dumpling looked like a squashed slipper. The filling oozed out of one side, and the pleats collapsed the moment she pressed them. Her cousin Jun snorted with laughter. “That one is going straight to the compost!” he teased. Mei-Ling’s cheeks burned as she glanced at the tray in front of her, where dozens of flawless dumplings stood in rows like tiny white boats.

“Take no notice of him,” Po Po said gently. “When I was your age, mine burst open in the water. Your fingers will learn; it only takes a little patience.” She demonstrated again, slowly, and Mei-Ling copied every movement with fierce concentration. By the tenth dumpling the pleats had begun to hold, and by the twentieth she was humming along to the music on the radio.

Then Po Po held up a shiny silver coin between finger and thumb. “Every year, we hide one of these inside a single dumpling,” she explained. “Whoever finds it will have good luck for the whole year.” While the children watched, she wrapped the coin in dough and shuffled it into the tray, so that nobody could possibly tell which dumpling contained it.

When the dumplings emerged from the steaming pot, everybody crowded around the table, and the kitchen filled with the smell of ginger and warm dough. Mei-Ling chose one at random and bit into it. Something hard clicked against her teeth. She drew out the coin, gleaming and wet, and held it up in astonishment.

“Mei-Ling has the luck!” cried her aunt, and the whole room applauded. Jun stared at her, and then, to her surprise, he grinned. “Was that one of the squashed ones?” he asked. Mei-Ling looked down at the little dumpling on her plate, which was lopsided, with the pleats undone at one end. “It was,” she said. Po Po smiled a secret smile and passed her the soy sauce.

title: Orangutans: Rainforest Rangers in Danger
text: Orangutans are large, reddish-brown apes that live in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, two islands in South-East Asia. Their name comes from two Malay words meaning “person of the forest”. When you watch an orangutan swinging through the branches, it is easy to see why.

Orangutans spend almost all of their lives high in the trees. Their arms are much longer than their legs, and an adult male can stretch his arms out to about two metres. Their hands and feet are strong and can grip like hooks. This helps them to climb slowly and carefully, reaching for branches that will hold their weight.

Most of an orangutan’s day is spent looking for food. They eat mainly fruit, but they also eat young leaves, bark, flowers and insects. Orangutans help the forest to grow. When they eat fruit, they swallow the seeds, and later they drop the seeds far away from the parent tree, where new trees can sprout. For this reason, they are sometimes called gardeners of the forest.

When night comes, each orangutan builds a new nest. It bends branches together and adds leaves to make a soft bed high above the ground. A mother orangutan looks after her baby for six or seven years, which is longer than any other animal apart from humans. During that time, the baby learns which fruits are safe to eat and how to build a nest of its own.

Sadly, all three kinds of orangutan are now critically endangered, which means they are at very high risk of disappearing from the wild. The biggest problem is that their forests are being cut down. Trees are cleared to make room for farms, and large areas have been turned into plantations of oil palms. Orangutans have less and less space to live in, and it is harder for them to find enough fruit.
Orangutans are also slow to have young. A mother may have only one baby every six to eight years, so their numbers cannot recover quickly.

Many people are working hard to help. Some groups protect areas of rainforest so that the trees cannot be cut down. Others care for orphaned babies in rescue centres, teach them the skills they need and then return them to the forest. Shoppers can help too, by choosing products made with palm oil that has been grown in ways that do not harm the rainforest. Every small choice makes a difference to the future of these clever, gentle apes.

title: How Rain Is Made
text: Every drop of rain that has ever fallen belongs to an endless journey known as the water cycle. Because the same water is used over and over again, the rain that fell on your school this morning may once have been part of a river, a puddle, or even the sea.

The journey begins with the Sun, whose heat warms the water in oceans, lakes and rivers. As the water warms, some of it changes into an invisible gas called water vapour, and this process is called evaporation. Although you cannot see vapour rising into the air, it is happening constantly, which is why puddles disappear on a sunny day.

Warm water vapour drifts upwards, and the higher it climbs, the colder the surrounding air becomes. When the vapour cools, it changes back into tiny droplets of liquid water. This change is known as condensation. You can observe it at home whenever steam from a hot bath meets a cold mirror and turns into a film of drops.

High in the sky, the droplets gather around minute specks of dust, and millions upon millions of them cluster together to form a cloud. Each droplet is so light that it is held up by the moving air. Clouds may look like solid cotton wool, but they are really made of water droplets and, where the air is very cold, tiny crystals of ice.

Inside the cloud, the droplets constantly collide and merge, so that they gradually grow larger. Eventually a drop becomes too heavy for the air to support, and it begins to fall. If the air beneath the cloud is warm enough, the drop reaches the ground as rain; if the air is freezing, it may arrive as snow or hail instead.

When the rain lands, some of it soaks into the soil, where plants absorb it through their roots. The rest runs across the ground into streams and rivers, which carry it back to the sea, and the whole journey can start again.

Different kinds of cloud bring different kinds of weather. Tall, thick, dark clouds usually hold the most water, because they contain vast numbers of droplets, and that is why the heaviest rain tends to fall from them. Thin, high clouds, on the other hand, are generally made of ice crystals, and they seldom produce rain at all.
Without the water cycle, there would be no fresh water for people, animals or plants. Rain may spoil a picnic, but it is one of the most valuable gifts that we receive from the sky.

title: Louis Braille and the Dots
text: Louis Braille was born in 1809 in the small French town of Coupvray, near Paris. His father made saddles and harnesses for horses, and Louis loved to watch him work in his workshop. When Louis was three years old, he picked up one of his father’s sharp tools and it slipped. The injury to his eye became infected, and soon both his eyes were badly harmed. By the time he was five, Louis could no longer see at all.

Louis was a bright, curious boy, and his family and neighbours helped him to learn. He listened carefully to his village priest and went to the village school, where he was often at the top of the class. When he was ten years old, he was awarded a place at a special school for blind children in Paris.

At the school, Louis was excited to find a library, but he was disappointed by the books. They were printed with large raised letters that pupils had to trace with their fingers. The letters were slow to read, and each book was heavy and huge. A single sentence could take a long time to work out. Louis longed for a faster way to read and to write.

One day, an army captain named Charles Barbier visited the school. He had invented a system he called “night writing”, which used patterns of twelve raised dots. Soldiers could read the messages with their fingertips in the dark, without needing a lamp or having to speak. However, the system was too complicated. Twelve dots were too many for a fingertip to feel at once.

Louis thought hard about the problem. He spent many hours at night in the workshop, pressing dots into paper with a sharp tool called an awl. At the age of fifteen, he found the answer. He cut the twelve dots down to six, arranged in two columns of three. Each letter of the alphabet could be made with a different pattern of dots, and one fingertip could feel a whole letter at once.

Louis went on to become a teacher at the school where he had once been a pupil. He also played the cello and the organ, and he even wrote music in his new dot system. In 1829, he published a book explaining how it worked. At first, many teachers did not want to use it, but pupils at the school loved it because it was quick and simple.

In the years that followed, the system spread across the world, and it was named Braille after its inventor. Today, blind and partly sighted people in almost every country still read books, labels and signs written in the dots that a fifteen-year-old boy first dreamed up.
